title: Polynomial-time additive-error estimation of output probabilities for shallow quantum circuits
abstract: We give a deterministic classical algorithm that estimates $|\langle x|U|0^n\rangle|^2$ to additive error $\varepsilon$ in $\mathrm{poly}(n, 1/\varepsilon)$ time, where $U$ is a constant-depth quantum circuit comprised of gates with bounded fan-in and arbitrary connectivity, and $x$ is an arbitrary $n$-bit output string. This improves over prior state-of-the-art algorithms that takes $n^{O(log(n))}$ time for the same task, $n^{O(log(log(n))}$ when $U$ is geometrically local, and $n^{O(1)}$ for 2D geometrically-local circuits.
summary:
**TL;DR** The authors give a deterministic classical algorithm that estimates the output probability of any constant-depth, bounded-fan-in quantum circuit with *arbitrary* connectivity to additive error ε in poly(n, 1/ε) time, removing the quasipolynomial n^{O(log n)} barrier of Bravyi–Gosset–Liu and the geometric-locality restriction of earlier polynomial-time results. The key move is an inclusion–exclusion decomposition that separates a small set of "bad" (non-peaked) output bits, handled by brute force, from the "good" bits, handled by a black-box cluster-expansion FPTAS expanded around the peaked computational basis state rather than the maximally mixed state.

**The big picture** Shallow quantum circuits are the main testbed for unconditional and conjectured quantum advantage, and a basic question is how hard it is classically to compute the probability of a specific measurement outcome to the same accuracy a quantum device would achieve with a modest number of repetitions. A decade of work chipped away at this, first for circuits laid out on two-dimensional grids, then for general grids and finally for arbitrary wiring but only at quasipolynomial cost. This paper closes the gap: for any fixed depth and gate size, the task is classically efficient regardless of how the qubits are connected. That removes one of the more natural candidate advantage tasks for shallow circuits — estimating a single outcome probability, which is more verification- and error-mitigation-friendly than sampling — from the list of plausibly hard problems.

**Key contributions**
- poly(n, 1/ε) deterministic additive estimation for depth-d, k-local circuits with arbitrary connectivity (previously n^{O(log n)}).
- A clean exact identity: P(0ⁿ) = Σ_T (−1)^{|T|} P(0_B, 1_T) · P(0_{T'}), where T ranges over good-bit sets whose connected components in the light-cone overlap graph touch the bad set B, and T' = [n] \ N_G[B ∪ T].
- A truncation bound showing the sum can be cut at |T| ≤ |B| + ⌈log₂(1/ε)⌉, via an entropy-style count of connected attachments (≤ 2^{|B|+s}(eK)^s) against decay τ^{s/(K+1)}.
- Generalization beyond circuits: any binary-variable distribution on a bounded-degree strong dependency graph with an exp(|S|)-time small-set oracle.
- Corollary: additive estimation of |⟨0ⁿ|U†(⊗Aᵢ)U|0ⁿ⟩| in poly time.

**How it works** Mark bit i "bad" if P(1ᵢ) > τ = (e²(2K+1))^{−(K+1)}, with K ≤ k^{2d} the max degree of the light-cone overlap graph. A pigeonhole/coloring argument over K+1 independent color classes shows P(0ⁿ) ≤ ε unless Σᵢ P(1ᵢ) < (K+1)log(1/ε), hence |B| = O(log(1/ε)). Then B ∪ T has size O(log 1/ε), so exact brute-force light-cone evaluation costs 2^{O(log 1/ε)} = poly(1/ε). The residual factor P(0_{T'}) is a marginal entirely on good bits, where every single-bit failure probability sits below the Mann–Waite threshold, so their cluster-expansion FPTAS gives relative error η in poly time; the appendix makes the log-truncation order m = ⌈log(2n/η)⌉ and connected-subgraph enumeration explicit.

**Why it matters** It sharpens the boundary of shallow-circuit advantage: outcome-probability estimation, unlike sampling, is now classically easy in full generality, so advantage claims must rest on sampling, relational problems, or depth/adaptivity. It also illustrates a useful template — doing cluster expansion around a peaked basis state instead of the identity — likely reusable elsewhere.

**Caveats** The constants are brutal: the ε-exponent scales as C_K(k^d + log K)log K with C_K = (K+1)[e²(2K+1)]^{K+1} and K ≤ k^{2d}, i.e. doubly exponential in depth, so this is asymptotic rather than practical. Additive estimates of individual probabilities need not form a normalized distribution; polynomial-time *sampling* for arbitrary-connectivity peaked shallow circuits remains open, as does recovering the sign or phase of general expectation values. Exact arithmetic is assumed, as in prior work.

title: Near-Optimal Ground-State Preparation without Controlled Hamiltonian Evolutions

\begin{abstract}
Ground-state preparation, energy estimation, and property estimation are fundamental tasks in quantum simulation.
Existing ground-state preparation algorithms achieve near-optimal complexity using block encodings or controlled Hamiltonian evolution, raising a natural question: is controlled Hamiltonian evolution necessary, or can the same scaling be attained in the weaker access model that provides access to only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution?
We resolve this question by giving two algorithms that access the input Hamiltonian $H$ only through queries to $U_H=\e^{-\iu H\tau}$ and its inverse $U_H^\dagger$, where $\|H\|\le\alpha_H$ and $\tau=\Theta(1/\alpha_H)$.
Given an input state with ground-state weight at least $\eta$ and a spectral gap of $H$ of at least $\gamma$, our first algorithm uses fresh copies of the input state and requires $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\eta))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, while our second algorithm uses coherent access to the input-state preparation unitary and its inverse to improve this complexity to $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$.
The latter bound matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that algorithms with additional access to controlled Hamiltonian evolution cannot improve the query complexity for ground-state preparation beyond logarithmic factors.
Both algorithms are based on a simple mechanism that we call the spectral descent principle, in which the algorithm starts from the input state $|\psi\rangle$ and progressively descends through the energy spectrum, moving closer to the ground state until the desired fidelity is reached.
We also extend this framework to ground-state property and energy estimation and give explicit complexity guarantees for both tasks.
\end{abstract}

\newpage

\tableofcontents

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Given a quantum Hamiltonian, preparing its ground state, determining its ground-state energy or estimating physical observables in that state are central tasks in quantum simulation.
These problems arise naturally in quantum chemistry, condensed-matter physics, and materials simulation, where ground-state energies determine quantities such as reaction energies and phase stability, while ground-state expectation values determine observables such as correlation functions, response properties, and molecular dipole moments~\cite{AspuruGuzik2005,Cao2019,McArdle2020,Bauer2020}. 
Ground-state preparation is also a basic subroutine
for other quantum simulation applications, like estimating Green's functions used in Dynamical Mean-Field Theory \cite{Ayral2025},
but also for purely quantum algorithmic applications like quantum linear algebra.

The difficulty is that these problems are computationally hard for a completely generic Hamiltonian. 
For example, deciding whether the ground-state energy of a local Hamiltonian lies below or above two promised thresholds is QMA-complete~\cite{Kitaev2002,Kempe2006}. 
The closely related problem of estimating a local observable in the ground state, formalized through the approximate-simulation problem APX-SIM, is in fact 
$\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{QMA}[\log]}$-complete~\cite{Ambainis2014,Gharibian2020}. 
Thus, an efficient ground-state algorithm cannot be expected without some prior information about the particular instance. 
To circumvent this hardness, standard algorithms assume we are provided with an initial state that has a non-negligible overlap with the true ground state~\cite{Poulin2009,Ge2019}. 
For example, in quantum chemistry one may initialize the algorithm with a Hartree-Fock or Kohn-Sham state, a small multi-determinant expansion, or a classically computed tensor-network state; such approximations are routinely used as trial states and can have substantial overlap with the true ground state~\cite{Berry2018,Fomichev2024,Berry2025}. 
Furthermore, tasks such as preparing the ground state or estimating observables in the ground state require the ground state to be distinguished from the rest of the spectrum~\cite{Lin2020,Dong2022,Zhang2022}. For these tasks, we additionally assume a known spectral gap. In practical scenarios, the spectral gap may be partially inferred from classical excited-state calculations or spectroscopic information about the system~\cite{Dreuw2005}.

To make these promises precise, let $H\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be a Hamiltonian with known spectral-norm bound $\|H\|\le\alpha_H$ and with spectral decomposition $H=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}E_j|\phi_j\rangle\langle\phi_j|$, where $\{|\phi_j\rangle\}_{j=0}^{d-1}$ are the eigenvectors of $H$ and the corresponding eigenvalues are ordered as $E_0<E_1\le\cdots\le E_{d-1}$. 
The ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$ is assumed to be unique. 
We are also given an input state $|\psi\rangle=\sum_jc_j|\phi_j\rangle$ whose ground-state weight (squared overlap) satisfies $|\langle\phi_0|\psi\rangle|^2=|c_0|^2\ge\eta$ for some known $\eta>0$. 
We refer to this as the \emph{overlap promise}. 
When coherent access to this state is needed, we assume black-box access to a preparation oracle $U_\psi$ and its inverse $U_\psi^\dagger$, where $U_\psi$ acts on an $n$-qubit system register, with $n=\lceil \log_2 d\rceil$, and satisfies $U_\psi|0^n\rangle=|\psi\rangle$. As discussed before, we are often given a \emph{gap promise}, i.e., a known spectral-gap lower bound $E_1-E_0\ge\gamma>0$. Note that we do not require these quantities to be known exactly: conservative lower bounds on the ground-state weight and the spectral gap are sufficient.

With the overlap and gap promises in place, we can now state the ground-state tasks considered in this work. 
In \emph{ground-state preparation} (GSP), both promises are given, and for a target infidelity $\xi\in(0,1)$ the goal is to output a state $\rho$ satisfying $\langle\phi_0|\rho|\phi_0\rangle\ge1-\xi$. 
In \emph{ground-state property estimation} (GSPE), an observable $O$ is additionally given and the goal is to estimate $\langle\phi_0|O|\phi_0\rangle$ to additive error $\varepsilon>0$. 
We assume that $O$ is specified classically in a form that admits an efficient measurement procedure, for example through an efficiently measurable Pauli decomposition. 
\textit{Ground-state energy estimation} (GSEE) asks instead for an estimate of $E_0$ to additive error $\varepsilon>0$. 
When the gap promise is available and $H$ itself can be efficiently measured from its classical description, GSEE is contained in the GSPE setting by taking the observable to be $H$, or equivalently $H/\alpha_H$ after normalization. 
GSEE can also be formulated under the overlap promise alone, without assuming a spectral gap, 
which is the reason behind keeping it separate from the other two. 
We will formally define these tasks later in \Cref{sec:ground-state-tasks}.

The computational complexity of these tasks depends on how the algorithm accesses the Hamiltonian $H$.
Our focus is the distinction between uncontrolled and controlled Hamiltonian evolution.
In the uncontrolled time-evolution model, the algorithm has access to $U_H\coloneqq \e^{-\iu H\tau}$ and its inverse $U_H^\dagger=\e^{+\iu H\tau}$ for a specified elementary time step $\tau>0$.
We count the total number $N_H$ of queries to these oracles and write $T_H=N_H\tau$ for the total Hamiltonian-evolution time.
For our algorithms, we choose $\tau=\Theta(1/\alpha_H)$.
On the other hand, the controlled time-evolution model additionally provides access to $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H\coloneqq |0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U_H$ and its inverse $(\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H)^\dagger$.
For a general black-box unitary, access to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$ does not imply access to $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$~\cite{Araujo2014}.
Controlled Hamiltonian evolution is therefore an additional oracle assumption.

Existing GSP algorithms achieve near-optimal complexity under stronger Hamiltonian-access assumptions.
Given an $\alpha_H$-block encoding $U_H^{\rm BE}$ of $H$, Lin and Tong gave a GSP algorithm using $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ queries to $U_H^{\rm BE}$, $(U_H^{\rm BE})^\dagger$, and their controlled versions~\cite{Lin2020}.\footnote{Throughout this paper, $\widetilde O(\cdot)$, $\widetilde \Omega(\cdot)$, and $\widetilde \Theta(\cdot)$ suppress polylogarithmic factors.}
For $\tau=\Theta(1/\alpha_H)$, the generic QET-U algorithm likewise uses $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ queries to $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$ and $(\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H)^\dagger$, corresponding to $\widetilde O(1/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ total Hamiltonian-evolution time~\cite{Dong2022}.
Concurrent work by Jeffery et al.~\cite{Jeffery2026} achieves optimal GSP query complexity using $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$ and $(\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H)^\dagger$.
Chen et al.~\cite{Chen2026} also obtain optimal query bounds using $U_H^{\rm BE}$, $(U_H^{\rm BE})^\dagger$, and their controlled versions, assuming a known energy threshold suitably located inside the spectral gap.

These results are now known to be optimal up to logarithmic factors, after the recent work by Somma and de Wolf~\cite{Somma2026} establishing an error-dependent lower bound that holds even when $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$ and $(\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H)^\dagger$ are available.
Translated into our notation, their result requires $\Omega(\alpha_H\log(1/\xi)/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ queries to $U_H$, $U_H^\dagger$, $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$, and $(\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H)^\dagger$ in total for worst-case GSP instances with $\tau=\Theta(1/\alpha_H)$.\footnote{Their GSP lower bound is stated in terms of trace-distance error $\varepsilon$.
For a target ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$ and an output state $\rho$, the trace distance satisfies
\begin{equation}
\frac12\left\|\rho-|\phi_0\rangle\langle\phi_0|\right\|_1 \le \sqrt{1-\langle\phi_0|\rho|\phi_0\rangle},
\end{equation}
where $\|\cdot\|_1$ denotes the trace norm.
Thus, the infidelity guarantee $1-\langle\phi_0|\rho|\phi_0\rangle\le\xi$ implies trace-distance error at most $\sqrt{\xi}$.
Applying their lower bound with $\varepsilon=\sqrt{\xi}$ and using $\log(1/\sqrt{\xi})=\tfrac12\log(1/\xi)$ gives the stated logarithmic dependence.}
The bound holds even when arbitrarily many queries to $U_\psi$ and $U_\psi^\dagger$ are free, and corresponds to $\Omega(\log(1/\xi)/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ total Hamiltonian-evolution time.

Our goal is to attain this lower bound up to logarithmic factors using only queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$.
This uncontrolled time-evolution model is the weakest of the three models discussed above: it provides neither a block encoding of $H$ nor access to $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$ or $(\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H)^\dagger$.
While QET-U removes controlled evolution for certain spin Hamiltonians by exploiting anticommutation properties, that construction does not extend to generic Hamiltonians satisfying only the standard overlap and gap promises~\cite{Dong2022}.

Removing the controlled Hamiltonian evolution is particularly relevant when the Hamiltonian dynamics is easier to realize than coherent control of the entire Hamiltonian evolution. 
On a fully fault-tolerant digital quantum computer, controlled Hamiltonian evolution can in principle be synthesized when a suitable circuit description of the simulation is available, but this generally introduces additional logical gates and coherent control. 
This overhead is especially relevant in the early fault-tolerant regime, where circuit depth remains limited and reducing the controlled structure of an algorithm is itself an important design objective~\cite{Dong2022,Zhang2022}.

The distinction is even more direct in analog and hybrid analog-digital quantum simulators. 
In these platforms, the desired many-body Hamiltonian is engineered physically and the system then evolves under that Hamiltonian, so ordinary uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution is a native operation rather than a digitally synthesized subroutine~\cite{Georgescu2014}. 
Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays realize tunable interacting spin Hamiltonians in this way~\cite{Bernien2017,Browaeys2020,Ebadi2021}. For example, an analog-Hamiltonian interface can directly program the coherent drive, detuning, and Rydberg interaction governing the atoms' many-body evolution \cite{wurtz2023aquila}. 
Long-range Ising dynamics is likewise implemented directly in trapped-ion quantum simulators~\cite{Zhang2017}, Hubbard-type Hamiltonians arise naturally in ultracold atoms in optical lattices~\cite{Esslinger2010,Schaefer2020}, and superconducting analog and analog-digital processors can realize interacting Bose-Hubbard or spin dynamics directly in hardware~\cite{Hangleiter2024,Andersen2025}. 
In all of these settings, native evolution under a Hamiltonian does not by itself supply an ancillary qubit that coherently switches the complete evolution on and off.

There has recently been growing interest in avoiding controlled Hamiltonian evolution in ground-state related tasks~\cite{Huggins2020,Lu2021,Russo2021,Schuckert2023,Hemery2024,Yang2024,Clinton2024,Chan2024,Lee2025,Kuji2025,Schwartzman2026,Patel2026}.
These approaches show that coherent control can often be avoided, but typically by exploiting additional structure, such as restricted variational ans\"atze, symmetries, or known reference eigenstates and eigenvalues.
Moreover, many of these works address energy or observable estimation rather than ground-state preparation itself; the few approaches aimed directly at GSP either rely on additional Hamiltonian structure~\cite{Dong2022} or do not provide a generic efficient algorithm with rigorous guarantees~\cite{Schwartzman2026}.
Thus, to the best of our knowledge, up to now there was no generic efficient GSP algorithm with optimal complexity that assumes only the standard overlap and gap promises and relies only on uncontrolled time-evolution oracles $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$.
Since efficient GSP can in turn be used to obtain ground-state property and energy-estimation algorithms, resolving this question also provides a general route to these tasks without controlled Hamiltonian evolution. This motivates the central question of this work:

\bigskip

\emph{Can we solve GSP using a near-optimal $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ number of queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$ in the uncontrolled time-evolution model, with $\tau=\Theta(1/\alpha_H)$, under only the standard spectral-gap and overlap promises?}

\subsection{Contributions}
\label{sec:contributions}

We answer this question affirmatively by giving two generic GSP algorithms in the uncontrolled time-evolution model.
For $\tau=\Theta(1/\alpha_H)$, our first algorithm, \emph{Spectral Descent} (SD), uses $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\eta))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$ with fresh-copy access to $|\psi\rangle$.
Our second algorithm, \emph{Coherent Spectral Descent} (CSD), uses $\widetilde O(\alpha_H/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$ with access to $U_\psi$ and $U_\psi^\dagger$.
Since the matching lower bound holds even when controlled Hamiltonian evolution is available~\cite{Somma2026}, CSD establishes that controlled evolution offers no improvement beyond logarithmic factors in the worst-case Hamiltonian-query complexity of GSP under coherent input-state access.
Our algorithms are based on a simple mechanism that we call the \emph{spectral descent principle}. 

\paragraph{Spectral Descent Principle.} A fundamental aspect of both algorithms is the use of two system registers. 
One is the \emph{anchor register}, which stores the current \emph{anchor state} that we seek to drive toward the ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$. 
The other is the \emph{candidate register}, which is prepared in the input state $|\psi\rangle$ and stores the \emph{candidate state}.
The basic idea is to compare these two states and update the anchor register with the candidate state only when the candidate state provides evidence of a lower-energy direction. 
We perform this comparison using an \emph{energy comparator} acting on the anchor register, candidate register, and a single \emph{witness qubit}. 
To understand this comparison spectrally, expand the anchor and candidate states in the eigenbasis of $H$, and consider a pair of eigenstate components $|\phi_a\rangle$ and $|\phi_b\rangle$, with respective energies $E_a$ and $E_b$.
The comparator effectively answers the question: is $E_b < E_a$ by a sufficient margin?
Crucially, it does this relative check without evaluating either $E_a$ or $E_b$ directly.
We measure the witness qubit in the computational basis $\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}$, where outcome $1$ indicates a \emph{witness}, meaning that the candidate state has sufficiently lower energy than the current anchor state, while outcome $0$ indicates \emph{no witness}.
Upon observing a witness, we swap the candidate and anchor registers.
By iteratively executing these successful updates, the anchor state monotonically descends through the energy spectrum until it reaches the ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$. 
This is why we refer to this mechanism as the spectral descent principle.
We describe this principle and its action on general anchor and candidate states in more detail in \Cref{sec:comparison-intuition}.

\paragraph{Energy Comparator and SWAP Echo.} The core technical challenge is implementing this energy comparator using only the uncontrolled oracles $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$. 
We solve this by introducing a new primitive that we refer to as the \emph{SWAP echo}.
For an anchor state and candidate state with energies $E_a$ and $E_b$ respectively, the SWAP echo interlaces forward and backward uncontrolled time evolution with controlled-SWAP gates (see \Cref{sec:swap-echo} for its circuit). 
This interference writes the relative energy difference $E_a-E_b$ directly into the phase of the witness qubit. 
We then process this relative phase using a Laurent quantum signal processing (QSP) sequence to construct the energy comparator. 
Because the QSP sequence only queries the SWAP echo directly, the entire comparator circuit does not require $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$.

\bigskip

Given that the candidate state $|\psi\rangle$ always possesses a ground-state component of weight at least $\eta$ from the overlap promise, an excited anchor state will trigger a successful downward update with a probability of order $\Omega(\eta)$. 
We present two variations of the algorithm that handle this success probability differently, depending on how the input state $|\psi\rangle$ is accessed.
Our first algorithm, SD, is designed for a weak input-state access model where the algorithm can only produce fresh copies of $|\psi\rangle$ and does not have access to its preparation unitary $U_\psi$. 
In each descent step, we prepare $|\psi\rangle$ in the candidate register, apply the energy comparator, and measure the witness qubit. 
If the measurement yields the outcome $0$ (no witness), we do not swap the anchor, discard the candidate register, and retry. 
Since every excited anchor component can pair with the ground-state component of the candidate state, each trial succeeds with a probability of order $\Omega(\eta)$. 
Therefore, $O(1/\eta)$ trials suffice to obtain an outcome 1 (witness) with constant probability.
This completes one descent step.
SD consists of multiple such descent steps.

\begin{theorem}[GSP via Spectral Descent, Informal]
\label{thm:intro-SD}
Assume the standard gap promise $\gamma$ and overlap promise $\eta$, and suppose we can prepare fresh copies of the input state $|\psi\rangle$. Then, the Spectral Descent algorithm (\Cref{alg:spectral-descent}) prepares a state $\rho$ satisfying $\langle\phi_0|\rho|\phi_0\rangle \ge 1-\xi$, using only the uncontrolled oracles $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, fresh preparations of $|\psi\rangle$, controlled-SWAP gates, and single-qubit operations.

By setting the elementary time step to $\tau = \Theta(1/\alpha_H)$, the algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(\alpha_H/(\gamma\eta))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, and uses $\widetilde{O}(1/\eta)$ fresh copies of $|\psi\rangle$. 
This corresponds to a total Hamiltonian-evolution time of $\widetilde{O}(1/(\gamma\eta))$. Crucially, the algorithm does not require access to~$\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$.
\end{theorem}

The $1/\eta$ factor in the query complexity for SD arises solely from repeatedly preparing and measuring the candidate state to find a witness. 
If instead we have access to the preparation oracles $U_\psi$ and $U_\psi^\dagger$, then, by exploiting amplitude amplification ideas, we can perform this search quadratically faster. 
Our second algorithm, CSD, is based on this stronger access model.
CSD employs the exact same anchor register, candidate register, SWAP echo, and energy comparator as SD. The only modification lies in how the witness is located. 
Instead of measuring the witness qubit and re-preparing the candidate state upon failure, CSD leaves the candidate register and witness qubit coherent. 
It applies the fixed-point amplitude amplification primitive of Ref.~\cite{Yoder2014} to the witness branch, amplifying the initial $\Omega(\eta)$ probability of seeing a witness to a constant using only $O(1/\sqrt{\eta})$ coherent applications of the energy comparator.
This completes one descent step, and, as with SD, CSD also consists of multiple such descent steps.

\begin{theorem}[GSP via Coherent Spectral Descent, Informal]
\label{thm:intro-CSD}
Assume the standard gap promise $\gamma$ and overlap promise $\eta$, and suppose we have coherent access to the state preparation oracle $U_\psi$ and its inverse $U_\psi^\dagger$. 
Then, the Coherent Spectral Descent algorithm prepares a state $\rho$ satisfying $\langle\phi_0|\rho|\phi_0\rangle \ge 1-\xi$, using only the uncontrolled oracles $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, the state oracles $U_\psi$ and $U_\psi^\dagger$, controlled-SWAP gates, and single-qubit operations. 

By setting the elementary time step to $\tau = \Theta(1/\alpha_H)$, the algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(\alpha_H/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, and uses $ \widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\eta})$ queries to $U_\psi$ and $U_\psi^\dagger$. 
This corresponds to a total Hamiltonian-evolution time of $\widetilde{O}(1/(\gamma\sqrt{\eta}))$. 
Crucially, the algorithm does not require access to~$\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$.
\end{theorem}

We now formalize these tasks (\Cref{sec:ground-state-tasks}) before introducing the 
spectral descent mechanism (\Cref{sec:comparison-intuition}), the SWAP echo (\Cref{sec:swap-echo}) and energy comparator (\Cref{sec:qsp-comparator}).
The main result concerning the spectral descent mechanism is presented in \Cref{sec:fresh-descent} and its coherent analogue in \Cref{sec:coherent-descent}. In addition, we also extend our result to ground-state property and energy estimation, with the corresponding theorems, complexity guarantees, and additional measurement-access assumptions given in \Cref{sec:ground-state-estimation}. Finally, we provide additional discussions in \Cref{sec:conclusions}.

\section{Ground-State Task Definitions}
\label{sec:ground-state-tasks}

We now formalize the ground-state tasks considered in this paper. 
Let $H\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be a Hamiltonian satisfying $\|H\|\le\alpha_H$, with spectral decomposition $H=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}E_j|\phi_j\rangle\langle\phi_j|$, where the eigenvalues are ordered as $E_0<E_1\le\cdots\le E_{d-1}$ and the ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$ is unique. We are additionally given an input state $|\psi\rangle=\sum_jc_j|\phi_j\rangle$.

\begin{promise}[Overlap promise]
\label{prom:overlap}
For a known parameter $\eta\in(0,1]$, the pair $(H,|\psi\rangle)$ satisfies the \emph{overlap promise} if the ground-state weight of $|\psi\rangle$ satisfies $|\langle\phi_0|\psi\rangle|^2=|c_0|^2\ge\eta$. Thus, $\eta$ is a known lower bound on the actual ground-state weight, which may be larger.
\end{promise}

\begin{promise}[Gap promise]
\label{prom:gap}
For a known parameter $\gamma>0$, the Hamiltonian $H$ satisfies the \emph{gap promise} if its ground-state spectral gap satisfies $E_1-E_0\ge\gamma$.
\end{promise}

With that in place, we next define the ground-state tasks.

\begin{problem}[Ground-State Preparation (GSP)]
\label{prob:gsp}
Given a Hamiltonian $H$ and an input state $|\psi\rangle$ satisfying Promises~\ref{prom:overlap} and~\ref{prom:gap}, together with a target infidelity $\xi\in(0,1)$, the \emph{ground-state preparation} (GSP) problem is to output a quantum state $\rho$ satisfying $\langle\phi_0|\rho|\phi_0\rangle\ge1-\xi$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Ground-State Property Estimation (GSPE)]
\label{prob:gspe}
Given a Hamiltonian $H$ and an input state $|\psi\rangle$ satisfying Promises~\ref{prom:overlap} and~\ref{prom:gap}, an observable $O$ satisfying $\|O\|\le1$, a target additive error $\varepsilon>0$, and a failure probability $\delta\in(0,1)$ the \emph{ground-state property estimation} (GSPE) problem is to output an estimate $\widehat \mu$ of $\mu \coloneqq \langle\phi_0|O|\phi_0\rangle$ satisfying $|\widehat \mu-\mu|\le\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Ground-State Energy Estimation (GSEE)]
\label{prob:gsee}
Given a Hamiltonian $H$ and an input state $|\psi\rangle$ satisfying Promise~\ref{prom:overlap}, together with a target additive error $\varepsilon>0$ and a failure probability $\delta\in(0,1)$, the \emph{ground-state energy estimation} (GSEE) problem is to output a classical estimate $\widehat E_0$ satisfying $|\widehat E_0-E_0|\le\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. Unlike GSP and GSPE as defined above, GSEE does not intrinsically require the gap promise.
\end{problem}

GSEE may be viewed as the special case of GSPE obtained by taking the observable $O$ to be $H/\alpha_H$. 
Nevertheless, we distinguish the two problems because GSEE can be posed under Promise~\ref{prom:overlap} alone, whereas the formulation of GSPE requires both Promises~\ref{prom:overlap} and~\ref{prom:gap}.

\section{The Spectral Descent Principle}
\label{sec:comparison-intuition}

Before presenting the SD and CSD algorithms, we first describe in more detail the common mechanism underlying both algorithms, which we refer to as the spectral descent principle.

Both algorithms operate on two system registers. 
The first is the \emph{anchor register}, which stores the current \emph{anchor state}, that is, the state the algorithm aims to iteratively improve and drive it towards the true ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$. 
The second is the \emph{candidate register}, which stores a \emph{candidate state} initialized to fresh copies of the input state $|\psi\rangle$.

To rigorously understand this principle, it is useful to begin with an idealized picture in which the anchor state happens to be an energy eigenstate $|\phi_a\rangle$ with eigenvalue $E_a$.
This is strictly for intuition; the algorithm does not assume access to energy eigenstates, nor does it project the anchor register into the energy basis.
The full algorithms and their analysis will later show how the same mechanism acts on a general anchor state.

Now prepare the candidate register in the input state $|\psi\rangle$. 
Writing $ |\psi\rangle=\sum_b c_b|\phi_b\rangle$ with $p_b=|c_b|^2$, the candidate state contains the energy component $|\phi_b\rangle$ with weight $p_b$.

For the moment, assume that we have access to an ideal energy comparison test, which we call the \emph{energy comparator}. 
Given the anchor state $|\phi_a\rangle$ and a candidate component $|\phi_b\rangle$, this ideal comparator flags a success, producing a \emph{witness}, if and only if the candidate energy is strictly lower than the anchor energy:
\begin{equation}
E_b < E_a. \label{eq:ideal-comparison-rule}
\end{equation}
Operationally, observing a witness guarantees that the candidate state contains a spectral component whose energy is closer to the ground state energy $E_0$ than the energy of the current anchor state.

We analyze the behavior of this rule in two distinct cases.
First, suppose the anchor state has already reached the ground state, so $a=0$. Because $E_0$ is the absolute minimum of the spectrum, there exists no candidate energy $E_b$ satisfying $E_b < E_0$. 
Consequently, the ideal comparator will never produce a witness:
\begin{equation}
\Pr[\text{witness} \mid a=0] = 0. \label{eq:ideal-ground-no-witness}
\end{equation}
This ensures stability: once the algorithm finds the ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$, it halts any further updates.

Second, suppose the anchor state is an excited state, meaning $a>0$. 
By the gap promise introduced earlier, we know that $E_a - E_0 \ge \gamma > 0$. 
Therefore, the strict inequality $E_0 < E_a$ is satisfied. 
This guarantees that the ground-state component $|\phi_0\rangle$ present in every fresh candidate state $|\psi\rangle$ will always trigger the witness condition in~\eqref{eq:ideal-comparison-rule}.

We can lower-bound the probability of observing this witness using the overlap promise.
The candidate state $|\psi\rangle$ possesses a ground-state weight $p_0 \ge \eta$. 
Because the ideal energy comparator deterministically produces a witness for this ground-state component whenever $a>0$, the overall probability of observing a witness is bounded by:
\begin{equation}
\Pr[\text{witness} \mid a>0] \ge p_0 \ge \eta. \label{eq:ideal-excited-witness}
\end{equation}
Other candidate components $|\phi_b\rangle$ with energies $E_b < E_a$ will also contribute to this probability, making~\eqref{eq:ideal-excited-witness} a strict lower bound. 
The important point here is that regardless of the complex structure of the excited spectrum, the ground-state component alone ensures a success probability of at least $\eta$ for any excited anchor state.

This inherent probabilistic separation shown by~\eqref{eq:ideal-ground-no-witness} and~\eqref{eq:ideal-excited-witness}, that is, zero witness probability for the ground state and at least $\eta$ for any excited state, dictates the update protocol for both SD and CSD. 
The procedure for a single update attempt is illustrated in \Cref{fig:spectral-descent-step}. 
We start with the current anchor state in register $A$, prepare a fresh candidate state $|\psi\rangle$ in register $B$, and apply the energy comparator alongside a single witness qubit $q$. 
If the measurement yields outcome $q=0$ (no witness), we discard the candidate register $B$, retain the state remaining in the anchor register $A$, and repeat the process with a newly prepared candidate state. 
If the measurement yields outcome $q=1$ (witness), we execute a SWAP operation to replace the current anchor state with the successful candidate state, and continue the descent from this newly updated anchor.

An unsuccessful comparison ($q=0$) therefore does not mean that the ground-state preparation has failed. 
It only means that the particular candidate state used in that comparison did not produce a useful downward update. 
The anchor state is neither discarded nor re-prepared. 
It remains stored in the anchor register and is compared with another fresh candidate state.
Furthermore, in the case when $q=1$, a successful candidate state also need not be the ground state. 
If the candidate state is now an intermediate eigenstate $|\phi_b\rangle$ such that
\begin{equation}
E_0 \le E_b < E_a,
\end{equation}
the condition~\eqref{eq:ideal-comparison-rule} is still met. 
Replacing the anchor state $|\phi_a\rangle$ with $|\phi_b\rangle$ successfully lowers the energy of the anchor register, even if it has not yet reached $E_0$. 
Subsequent successful comparisons will continue to drive the anchor energy downward.

The overlap promise ensures that an excited anchor state cannot become trapped at a local minimum. 
If the anchor state is fixed at an excited eigenstate $|\phi_a\rangle$, each independent attempt with a fresh candidate state $|\psi\rangle$ yields a downward witness with probability at least $\eta$, as established in~\eqref{eq:ideal-excited-witness}. 
Therefore, if we execute $M$ independent comparison trials, the probability of failing to obtain any witness decays exponentially:
\begin{equation}
\Pr[\text{no witness in } M \text{ trials}] \le (1-\eta)^M \le \mathrm{e}^{-\eta M}. \label{eq:ideal-M-failure}
\end{equation}
Consequently, executing $M = \mathcal{O}(1/\eta)$ repetitions guarantees a successful downward update with constant probability.

Notice that this rigorous bound relies exclusively on the ground-state component of $|\psi\rangle$. 
We do not require any assumptions about the gaps between adjacent excited states. 
The excited spectrum can be arbitrarily closely spaced or highly degenerate. 
The only spectral separation required is the initial gap promise $E_1 - E_0 \ge \gamma$, which guarantees that the target ground state $|\phi_0\rangle$ is safely separated from any excited anchor state $|\phi_a\rangle$.

Up to this point, our analysis has relied on an ideal energy comparator that perfectly evaluates the strict inequality $E_b < E_a$. 
Also an algorithm must execute this relative comparison without measuring the registers in the energy basis and without utilizing $\mathrm{ctrl}\text{-}U_H$. 
To construct this practical comparator, we begin by introducing a new primitive in the next section called the \emph{SWAP echo}.

\section{The SWAP Echo}
\label{sec:swap-echo}

Let $A$ denote the anchor register and $B$ the candidate register. 
Define the two-register difference Hamiltonian as follows:
\begin{equation}
D_{AB}\coloneqq H_A \otimes I_B - I_A \otimes H_B. \label{eq:DAB}
\end{equation}
This Hamiltonian is useful because, on a joint energy eigenstate $|\phi_a\rangle_A|\phi_b\rangle_B$, it acts as
\begin{equation}
D_{AB} |\phi_a\rangle_A |\phi_b\rangle_B = (E_a - E_b) |\phi_a\rangle_A |\phi_b\rangle_B.
\end{equation}
Thus the eigenvalue of $D_{AB}$ is exactly the quantity needed for the energy comparison.

At first sight, implementing evolution under $D_{AB}$ for some time $\tau$ might appear nontrivial.
In fact, it follows directly from the fact that $H_A$ and $H_B$ act on different registers, they commute, and therefore
\begin{equation}
\e^{-\iu D_{AB}\tau} = \e^{-\iu H_A\tau}\otimes\e^{+\iu H_B\tau}. \label{eq:difference-evolution-factorization}
\end{equation}
 

This gives access to the phase $\e^{-\iu(E_a-E_b)\tau}$, but by itself it does not place that phase on some signal qubit that we can eventually process. 
For the energy comparator, we want a qubit whose two computational-basis states see opposite signs of the energy difference. 
A controlled-SWAP operation provides exactly the required mechanism.

Introduce a signal qubit $q$, and let
\begin{equation}
\cSWAP \coloneqq |0\rangle\!\langle0|_q\otimes I_{AB} + |1\rangle\!\langle1|_q\otimes\operatorname{SWAP}_{AB}, \label{eq:controlled-swap}
\end{equation}
denote the controlled-SWAP operation.
Now consider the following sequence. 
First apply $\cSWAP$ on all registers, then evolve $A$ forward and $B$ backward, and finally apply the $\cSWAP$ again on all registers (see \Cref{fig:echo} for its circuit, ignoring the first phase rotation gate on $q$). 
Formally, we denote this sequence as
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO(\tau) \coloneqq \cSWAP \bigl(I_q\otimes \e^{-\iu D_{AB}\tau} \bigr)\cSWAP . \label{eq:W}
\end{equation}

One can easily understand the role of the two $\cSWAP$s by following the two branches of the signal qubit. 
If $q=0$, neither $\cSWAP$ acts, so the two system registers undergo $\e^{-\iu D_{AB}\tau}$. 
If $q=1$, the first $\cSWAP$ exchanges $A$ and $B$ before the evolution. 
The forward evolution is therefore applied to what was originally the candidate register, while the backward evolution is applied to what was originally the anchor register. 
The second $\cSWAP$ restores the registers to their original locations. 
The net effect is to reverse the sign of the difference Hamiltonian, giving $\e^{+\iu D_{AB}\tau}$.
The resulting operation is therefore an exact qubit-controlled sign choice for the difference Hamiltonian.

\begin{lemma}[Energy-difference signal]
\label{lem:exact-signal}
The SWAP echo in~\eqref{eq:W} satisfies
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO(\tau) = |0\rangle\langle0|_q\otimes\e^{-\iu D_{AB}\tau} + |1\rangle\langle1|_q\otimes\e^{+\iu D_{AB}\tau} = \e^{-\iu Z_q\otimes D_{AB}\tau}, \label{eq:W-exact}
\end{equation}
where $Z_q$ is the Pauli-Z operator acting on the signal qubit $q$.
Furthermore, for any classically known scalar shift $s \in \mathbb{R}$, applying an initial single-qubit phase rotation $e^{-i s \tau Z_q}$ yields the ``shifted SWAP echo":
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO_s(\tau) \coloneqq \e^{-\iu s\tau Z_q}\SWAPECHO(\tau) = \e^{-\iu Z_q\otimes(D_{AB}+sI)\tau}. \label{eq:Ws}
\end{equation}
The quantum circuit for $\SWAPECHO_s(\tau)$ is provided in \Cref{fig:echo}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
See~\Cref{sec:proof-of-exact-signal-lemma}.    
\end{proof}

Suppose, following the intuition of the previous section, that the anchor state has energy $E_a$ and the candidate state has energy $E_b$. 
Since $D_{AB}$ has eigenvalue $E_a-E_b$ on this pair, the shifted SWAP echo $\SWAPECHO_s(\tau)$ acts on the signal qubit $q$ as
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO_s(\tau) |q\rangle|\phi_a\rangle|\phi_b\rangle = \e^{-\iu(E_a-E_b+s)\tau z_q} |q\rangle|\phi_a\rangle|\phi_b\rangle, \label{eq:signal-on-eigenpair}
\end{equation}
where $z_q=+1$ for $q=0$ and $z_q=-1$ for $q=1$.

Thus the two energies $E_a$ and $E_b$ never need to be measured individually. 
Their difference appears directly as opposite phases on the two signal-qubit branches,
\begin{equation}
\e^{-\iu(E_a-E_b+s)\tau} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \e^{+\iu(E_a-E_b+s)\tau}.
\end{equation}
The shift $s$ allows us to choose where the comparison threshold lies. In the next section, we choose $s$ so that “candidate not below the anchor” and “candidate lower by at least $\gamma$” lie on opposite sides of the phase threshold.
Finally, it is important to note that $\SWAPECHO_s(\tau)$ does not use any ctrl-$U_H$. 

\section{Energy Comparator}
\label{sec:qsp-comparator}

The SWAP echo from the previous section gives us the quantity we need for energy comparison, but not yet in the form required by our SD and CSD algorithms. 
For a given pair of energy eigenstates $|\phi_a\rangle_A|\phi_b\rangle_B$, we must process this phase so that the signal qubit acts as a binary indicator, explicitly flagging when the candidate state has a sufficiently lower energy than the anchor state.

More precisely, if the candidate state energy is higher than or equal to the anchor state energy ($E_b\ge E_a$), the energy comparator must almost never produce a witness. 
On the other hand, if the candidate state energy is lower than the anchor state energy by at least the promised gap $\gamma$, that is, $E_a-E_b\ge\gamma$, then it should produce a witness with high probability. 
We do not need to decide what happens sharply for the intermediate case when $0<E_a-E_b<\gamma$. 
In particular, the energy comparator does not need to resolve arbitrarily small spacings between excited energies.

We therefore aim to construct a \emph{soft energy comparator}, rather than the ideal energy comparator discussed previously in \Cref{sec:comparison-intuition}.
For a chosen error parameter $\zeta>0$, let $r_{ab}$ denote the witness probability of this comparator, namely, the probability of obtaining the outcome $q=1$.
We require that $r_{ab}$ satisfy
\begin{align}
E_a-E_b\le0 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{ab}\le\zeta, \label{eq:soft-comparator-left} \\
E_a-E_b\ge\gamma &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{ab}\ge1-\zeta. \label{eq:soft-comparator-right}
\end{align}
The transition between these two regimes is allowed to be smooth.
We construct this comparator using $\SWAPECHO_s(\tau)$ defined in~\eqref{eq:Ws} in two steps. 
First, we choose the shift $s$ and evolution time $\tau$ so that the two regimes in~\eqref{eq:soft-comparator-left}--\eqref{eq:soft-comparator-right} map to separated regions of a nonaliased phase interval. 
We then approximate a smooth transition between these regions and realize the resulting witness probability using Laurent quantum signal processing (Laurent QSP) applied directly to the $\SWAPECHO_s(\tau)$.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Choosing the Shift $s$ and Evolution Time $\tau$}{Choosing the Shift s and Evolution Time tau}}

We begin by placing the two comparison regimes in~\eqref{eq:soft-comparator-left}--\eqref{eq:soft-comparator-right} symmetrically around zero. 
The shifted echo $\SWAPECHO_s(\tau)$ allows us to add any known scalar $s$ to the energy difference. 
We choose $s=-\gamma/2$, so that the midpoint between the two relevant thresholds, $E_a-E_b=0$ and $E_a-E_b=\gamma$, is mapped to zero.

With this specific shift, we define the gap-shifted SWAP echo as
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO_\gamma(\tau) \coloneqq \e^{+\iu(\gamma\tau/2)Z_q}\SWAPECHO(\tau) = \e^{-\iu Z_q\otimes(D_{AB}-\gamma I/2)\tau}. \label{eq:Wgamma}
\end{equation}
When applied to the energy eigenstate pair $|\phi_a\rangle_A|\phi_b\rangle_B$, this operator generates a shifted relative phase given by
\begin{equation}
\theta_{ab} \coloneqq \tau\left( E_a-E_b-\frac{\gamma}{2} \right). \label{eq:theta-ab}
\end{equation}
This shift correctly places the two regimes on strictly opposite sides of zero:
\begin{align}
E_a-E_b\le0 &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\le-\frac{\gamma\tau}{2}, \label{eq:soft-comparator-left-theta} \\
E_a-E_b\ge\gamma &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\ge+\frac{\gamma\tau}{2}. \label{eq:soft-comparator-right-theta}
\end{align}

Next, we choose the evolution time $\tau$. 
Because the signal is a phase, energy differences that wrap around the unit circle could become ambiguous. 
We therefore restrict all occupied phases to a single interval on which the ordering of energy differences is preserved.
Note that $|E_a-E_b|\le 2 \|H\| \leq 2 \alpha_H$
for every energy pair that can occur in the two system registers. 
After the shift by $-\gamma/2$, this gives $|E_a-E_b-\sfrac{\gamma}{2}| \le 2 \alpha_H +\sfrac{\gamma}{2}$.
With that, we choose
\begin{equation}
\tau \coloneqq \frac{\pi}{4\left(2 \alpha_H+\frac{\gamma}{2}\right)}. \label{eq:tau}
\end{equation}
Then every occupied energy pair satisfies $|\theta_{ab}| \le \tau (2 \alpha_H+\sfrac{\gamma}{2}) = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
Hence all relevant phases lie in the interval $[-\pi/4,\pi/4]$. 
This prevents phase wrapping and, equally importantly, gives us an interval on which a simple real function of the phase is monotone.

We therefore define
\begin{equation}
y_{ab} \coloneqq \sin(2\theta_{ab}), \qquad \Delta \coloneqq \sin(\tau\gamma). \label{eq:y-and-Delta}
\end{equation}
Note that the function $\sin(2\theta)$ is monotone increasing on $[-\pi/4,\pi/4]$. 
Therefore the ordering established above in~\eqref{eq:soft-comparator-left-theta}--\eqref{eq:soft-comparator-right-theta} is preserved:
\begin{align}
E_a-E_b\le0 &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\le-\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\le-\Delta, \label{eq:y-left} \\
E_a-E_b\ge\gamma &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\ge+\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\ge+\Delta. \label{eq:y-right}
\end{align}
The energy-comparison problem has thus been reduced to distinguishing two well-separated regions of a real variable $y_{ab}$: values satisfying $y_{ab} \le -\Delta$ must yield a low witness probability, while values satisfying $y_{ab} \ge +\Delta$ must yield a high witness probability.
The parameter $\Delta$ determines how difficult this approximation will be. 
Using the fact that $\sin u\ge 2u/\pi$ for $u\in[0,\pi/2]$, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Delta-lower} \Delta \ge\frac{2\tau\gamma}{\pi}=\frac{\gamma}{2\left(2 \alpha_H+\frac{\gamma}{2}\right)}.
\end{equation}
The next subsection constructs a bounded soft step function across this separation and then approximates it by a polynomial suitable for QSP.

\subsection{Soft Energy Comparison Probability}
\label{sec:soft-comparator}

Fix a target energy comparator error $\zeta\in(0,1/4)$. 
We now choose the probability with which the signal qubit should indicate a witness as a function of the real signal variable $y$.

A sharp step at $y=0$ would reproduce the ideal comparison rule, but such a discontinuous function cannot be implemented exactly by a finite-degree polynomial. 
It is also unnecessary for spectral descent. 
We only require a small witness probability when $y\le-\Delta$ and a large witness probability when $y\ge+\Delta$; inside the transition region $(-\Delta,\Delta)$, the probability may vary smoothly.

We additionally require this variation to be monotone. 
For a fixed anchor state, a candidate state lying farther below it in energy corresponds to a larger value of $y$. 
Its witness probability should therefore not be smaller. 
This monotonicity will later be used to show that conditioning on a witness biases the candidate state toward lower energies.

For this purpose, we employ the following smooth function of $y$:
\begin{equation}
r_\star(y) \coloneqq \frac{1+\operatorname{erf}(\kappa y)}{2}, \qquad \kappa \coloneqq \frac{1}{\Delta} \sqrt{\log\frac{8}{\zeta}}. \label{eq:rstar}
\end{equation}
Note that the function $r_\star$ is monotone increasing, with values between $0$ and $1$. 
The parameter $\kappa$ controls how rapidly it changes around $y=0$. 
Because $\kappa$ scales as $1/\Delta$, the transition becomes sharper when the two comparison regions are closer together.
The particular constant in the definition of $\kappa$ is chosen so that the two regions already have a comfortable error margin before any polynomial approximation is introduced. 

Using the standard bound $\operatorname{erf}(u)\ge 1-\e^{-u^2}$ for $u\ge0$ in~\eqref{eq:rstar}, we obtain
\begin{align}
E_a-E_b\le0 &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\le-\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\le-\Delta \Longrightarrow r_\star(y) \le \frac{\zeta}{16}, \label{eq:rstar-left} \\
E_a-E_b\ge\gamma &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\ge+\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\ge+\Delta \Longrightarrow r_\star(y) \ge 1-\frac{\zeta}{16}. \label{eq:rstar-right}
\end{align}
Thus $r_\star$ already behaves as the desired soft energy comparator, with some room left for polynomial approximation error.

The remaining issue is that $r_\star$ is not itself a polynomial, whereas its Laurent-QSP construction, which we will present in the next section, requires a bounded polynomial of $y$. 
We therefore state the approximation result in the following lemma that we will use later.

\begin{lemma}[Polynomial approximation of $r_\star$]
\label{lem:soft-comparator-polynomial}
For every $\zeta\in(0,1/4)$, there exists a real polynomial $\widetilde r$ of degree
$O(\sfrac{1}{\Delta}\log\sfrac{1}{\zeta})$
such that $0\le\widetilde r(y)\le1$ for every $y\in[-1,1]$ and
\begin{equation}
\sup_{y\in[-1,1]} \left| \widetilde r(y)-r_\star(y) \right| \le \frac{\zeta}{32}. \label{eq:rtilde-monotone-close}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
    See~\Cref{app:soft-comparator-polynomial}.
\end{proof}

Combining \Cref{lem:soft-comparator-polynomial} with
\eqref{eq:rstar-left}--\eqref{eq:rstar-right}, we obtain
\begin{align}
E_a-E_b\le0 &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\le-\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\le-\Delta \Longrightarrow r_\star(y_{ab}) \le \frac{\zeta}{16}\Longrightarrow \widetilde r(y_{ab})\le\zeta, \label{eq:rtilde-left} \\
E_a-E_b\ge\gamma &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\ge+\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\ge+\Delta \Longrightarrow r_\star(y_{ab}) \ge 1-\frac{\zeta}{16}\Longrightarrow \widetilde r(y_{ab})\ge1-\zeta. \label{eq:rtilde-right}
\end{align}
Thus $\widetilde r(y)$ has exactly the behavior required of the witness probability.
Finally, using~\eqref{eq:Delta-lower}, the degree bound in~\Cref{lem:soft-comparator-polynomial} becomes $O((\alpha_H/\gamma+1)\log(1/\zeta))$.

The polynomial $\widetilde r$ specifies the witness probability we want, but we have not yet shown that a quantum circuit constructed using the SWAP echo can realize this probability. 
The next step is to connect $\widetilde r(y)$ to Laurent QSP.

\subsection{Realizing the Soft Energy Comparator with Laurent QSP}
\label{sec:laurent-qsp-synthesis}

Recall that for an energy pair $|\phi_a\rangle_A|\phi_b\rangle_B$, the shifted SWAP echo $\SWAPECHO_\gamma(\tau)$ supplies the phase $\theta_{ab}$ given in~\eqref{eq:theta-ab}.
We aim to construct a circuit that produces a witness outcome with probability $\widetilde{r}(y_{ab})$, where $y_{ab} = \sin(2\theta_{ab})$.

To connect this real variable to the Laurent-QSP signal, let $t\coloneqq\e^{\iu\theta}$ and $z\coloneqq t^2=\e^{2\iu\theta}.$
Then $\sin(2\theta) = \sfrac{(z-z^{-1})}{2\iu}.$
Consequently, the target probability polynomial $\widetilde{r}(y)$ can be mapped to a Laurent polynomial in $z$, which we define as
\begin{equation}
\mathcal R(z) \coloneqq \widetilde r\!\left( \frac{z-z^{-1}}{2\iu} \right). \label{eq:R-Laurent}
\end{equation}
Because $\widetilde{r}(y)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, $\mathcal{R}(z)$ is a Laurent polynomial of degree at most $n$ in $z$. 
Moreover, from the range of $\widetilde r$ given in the statement of \Cref{lem:soft-comparator-polynomial}, we get $0\le\mathcal R(z)\le1$ for $|z|=1$.

We next relate this Laurent variable $z$ to the gap-shifted SWAP echo. 
On the fixed energy pair $|\phi_a\rangle_A|\phi_b\rangle_B$,~\eqref{eq:Wgamma} and~\eqref{eq:theta-ab} give
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO_\gamma(\tau)\big|_{a,b} = \e^{-\iu\theta_{ab}Z_q} = \begin{pmatrix} \e^{-\iu\theta_{ab}} & 0\\ 0 & \e^{+\iu\theta_{ab}} \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Defining $t_{ab}\coloneqq\e^{\iu\theta_{ab}}$, we can rewrite this as
\begin{equation}
\SWAPECHO_\gamma(\tau)\big|_{a,b} = \begin{pmatrix} t_{ab}^{-1} & 0\\ 0 & t_{ab} \end{pmatrix}. \label{eq:physical-Vt}
\end{equation}
This is precisely the signal form used by Laurent QSP: repeated applications of the SWAP echo generate powers of $t_{ab}$ and $t_{ab}^{-1}$, while interleaved single-qubit rotations acting on $q$ combine these powers into the desired Laurent polynomial.
Then since $z=t^2$, we have
$z_{ab} = t_{ab}^2 = \e^{2\iu\theta_{ab}},$
and hence
\begin{equation}
\mathcal R(z_{ab}) = \widetilde r\!\left( \frac{t_{ab}^2-t_{ab}^{-2}}{2\iu} \right) = \widetilde r\!\left( \sin(2\theta_{ab}) \right) = \widetilde r(y_{ab}). \label{eq:R-physical}
\end{equation}
Thus the probability polynomial constructed in the previous subsection is a Laurent polynomial of the phase variable supplied directly by the SWAP echo.

We formally state this required synthesis in the following lemma using the Laurent-QSP product-decomposition
theorem~\cite[Theorem~2]{Haah2019}.

\begin{lemma}[Laurent-QSP realization of $\widetilde{r}$]
\label{lem:laurent-qsp-comparator}
Let $\widetilde{r}(y)$ be the degree-$n$ polynomial defined in \Cref{lem:soft-comparator-polynomial}. 
There exists a unitary circuit $C_\zeta$, constructed using at most $2n$ queries to the shifted SWAP echo $\SWAPECHO_\gamma(\tau)$ interleaved with single-qubit gates on $q$, such that its action on any occupied energy pair is
\begin{equation}
C_\zeta |0\rangle_q |\phi_a\rangle_A |\phi_b\rangle_B = A(z_{ab}) |0\rangle_q |\phi_a\rangle_A |\phi_b\rangle_B + B(z_{ab}) |1\rangle_q |\phi_a\rangle_A |\phi_b\rangle_B, \label{eq:comparator-action}
\end{equation}
where $z_{ab} = e^{2i\theta_{ab}}$, and the amplitude coefficient explicitly satisfies
\begin{equation}
|B(z_{ab})|^2 = \mathcal{R}(z_{ab}) = \widetilde{r}(y_{ab}). \label{eq:qsp-witness-probability}
\end{equation}
Crucially, this circuit only queries $\SWAPECHO_\gamma(\tau)$ directly and does not require controlled access to it.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
See~\Cref{app:laurent-qsp-synthesis}.
\end{proof}

We take $q=1$ to be the witness outcome and define its probability by
\begin{equation}
r_{ab} \coloneqq \Pr[q=1\mid a,b] = |B(z_{ab})|^2 = \widetilde r(y_{ab}). \label{eq:rab}
\end{equation}
The construction developed across the previous subsections can now be read as a direct chain from the energy difference to this witness probability:
\begin{align}
E_a-E_b\le0 &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\le-\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\le-\Delta \Longrightarrow r_{ab}\le\zeta, \label{eq:pair-pass} \\
E_a-E_b\ge\gamma &\Longleftrightarrow \theta_{ab}\ge+\frac{\gamma\tau}{2} \Longleftrightarrow y_{ab}\ge+\Delta \Longrightarrow r_{ab}\ge1-\zeta. \label{eq:pair-reject}
\end{align}
These are exactly the two comparison guarantees required by spectral descent.

We will also need the behavior of the comparator inside the transition region $0<E_a-E_b<\gamma$. 
Although no sharp decision is required there, the physical witness probability should remain close to a monotone function of the energy difference. 
Using~\eqref{eq:theta-ab}, we view the smooth target from~\eqref{eq:rstar} as
\begin{equation}
r_\star(E_a-E_b) \coloneqq r_\star\!\left( \sin\left[ 2\tau\left( E_a-E_b-\frac{\gamma}{2} \right) \right] \right). \label{eq:rstar-energy}
\end{equation}
Since all occupied phases lie in $[-\pi/4,\pi/4]$, the inner sine is monotone increasing in $E_a-E_b$, and $r_\star$ is itself monotone increasing. 
Thus $r_\star(E_a-E_b)$ is monotone throughout the occupied spectral range. 
Using the uniform approximation bound from~\eqref{eq:rtilde-monotone-close}, the physical witness probability tightly tracks this monotonic curve:
\begin{equation}
\left| r_{ab} - r_\star(E_a - E_b) \right| \le \frac{\zeta}{32}. \label{eq:rab-monotone-close}
\end{equation}
This property will later be used to show that conditioning on a witness biases the candidate state toward lower energies.

We summarize the energy comparator $C_\zeta$ and its cost below.

\begin{theorem}[Energy comparator cost]
\label{thm:qsp-filter}
For every $\zeta\in(0,1/4)$, there exists a unitary comparator circuit $C_\zeta$ whose witness probability $r_{ab}$ satisfies the strict comparison bounds in~\eqref{eq:pair-pass} and~\eqref{eq:pair-reject}, and the monotonic tracking bound in~\eqref{eq:rab-monotone-close} for all occupied energy pairs.
The comparator $C_\zeta$ uses
\begin{equation}
d = O\!\left( \left( \frac{\alpha_H}{\gamma}+1 \right) \log\frac{1}{\zeta} \right) \label{eq:qsp-degree}
\end{equation}
SWAP-echo queries, with sequential Hamiltonian-evolution time
\begin{equation}
T_{\rm cmp} = O\!\left( \frac{1}{\gamma} \log\frac{1}{\zeta} \right). \label{eq:qsp-comparator-time}
\end{equation}
The construction requires no ctrl-$\e^{-\iu Ht}$.
\end{theorem}

The scaling of the total evolution time $T_{\mathrm{cmp}}$ relies on the following argument. 
While the total number of SWAP-echo queries $d$ scales proportionally to $\alpha_H/\gamma$, each individual query applies time evolution for an elementary duration $\tau = \Theta(1/(\alpha_H + \gamma))$. 
Consequently, the dependence on $\alpha_H$ cancels out in the product $\Theta(d\tau)$, yielding a total evolution time proportional to $\gamma^{-1} \log(1/\zeta)$.

\section{Spectral Descent}
\label{sec:fresh-descent}

We now use the energy comparator $C_\zeta$ to turn the spectral descent principle of \Cref{sec:comparison-intuition} into an explicit ground-state preparation algorithm called Spectral Descent (SD).
This algorithm relies on a weak access model for the input state; that is, we assume that we have the ability to prepare fresh copies of the state $|\psi\rangle$ and do not have access to $U_\psi$.

SD maintains two system registers: the anchor register $A$ stores the current anchor state, while the candidate register $B$ is repeatedly prepared in the input state $|\psi\rangle$. 
One application of $C_\zeta$ to registers $A$, $B$, and the witness qubit $q$ is what we refer to as a \emph{comparison trial}. 
After each trial, SD measures the witness qubit $q$ in the computational basis $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$.
In what follows, the notation $q=0$ or $q=1$ refers to the corresponding classical measurement outcome, while $q$ by itself denotes the witness qubit.
If the outcome is $q=1$ (witness), the candidate and anchor registers are swapped. 
If the outcome is $q=0$ (no witness), the candidate register is discarded and the algorithm proceeds with the state remaining in the anchor register.

A sequence of at most $M$ comparison trials is what we refer to as a \emph{descent stage}. 
A stage ends as soon as the first witness outcome $q=1$ is observed, or after $M$ trials if no witness is found. 
The algorithm performs $R$ such stages.

\subsection{Spectral Descent Algorithm}
\label{sec:measured-algorithm}

The complete procedure is given in \Cref{alg:spectral-descent}. 
The parameter choices for $\zeta, M$, and $R$ appearing in Step 1 of the algorithm will be justified in \Cref{sec:convergence-sd}.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Spectral Descent (SD)}
\label{alg:spectral-descent}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Statex \hspace{-\algorithmicindent} \textbf{Input:} Fresh-copy access to the input state $|\psi\rangle$; known overlap lower bound $\eta$; known gap lower bound $\gamma$; target infidelity $\xi\in(0,1)$.

\Statex \hspace{-\algorithmicindent} \textbf{Output:} An anchor state $\rho_R$ satisfying $\langle\phi_0|\rho_R|\phi_0\rangle\ge 1-\xi$.

\State Set
\begin{equation}

\end{equation}
\State Construct the energy comparator $C_\zeta$ from
\Cref{sec:qsp-comparator}.
\State Prepare the anchor register $A$ in the state $|\psi\rangle$.

\For{$t=1,\ldots,R$}
    \For{$m=1,\ldots,M$}
        \State Prepare the candidate register $B$ in the state
        $|\psi\rangle$.
        \State Initialize the witness qubit $q$ in $|0\rangle$.
        \State Apply $C_\zeta$ to joint register $qAB$.
        \State Measure $q$ in the computational basis $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$.

            \State Apply $\operatorname{SWAP}_{AB}$, so that the
            accepted candidate becomes the new anchor.
            \State Discard $B$ and reset $q$.
            \State Terminate the current descent stage.
        \Else
            \State Discard $B$ and reset $q$.
        \EndIf
    \EndFor
\EndFor

\State \Return the state $\rho_R$ in the anchor register $A$.
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

**TL;DR** The paper gives the first generic ground-state preparation algorithm that queries the Hamiltonian only through uncontrolled forward/backward time evolution, achieving Õ(α_H/(γ√η)) queries — matching the known lower bound (which holds even with controlled evolution) up to logs. The key primitive is a "SWAP echo": sandwiching e^{-iHτ}⊗e^{+iHτ} on two system copies between two controlled-SWAPs exactly realizes e^{-i Z_q ⊗ (H_A - H_B) τ}, converting a *control on the Hamiltonian* into a *control on a SWAP*.

**The big picture** Most near-optimal quantum algorithms for finding ground states require the ability to turn the Hamiltonian's time evolution on and off coherently, conditioned on an ancilla qubit. On analog and hybrid analog-digital simulators, and in early fault-tolerant settings, that kind of coherent control is expensive or simply unavailable, while plain evolution under the engineered Hamiltonian is native. This work shows that the extra control buys nothing asymptotically: by running two copies of the system and comparing their energies interferometrically, one can prepare ground states with the same optimal cost using only ordinary evolution forward and backward in time.

**Key contributions**
- The SWAP echo primitive: an exact, control-free implementation of qubit-conditioned evolution under the difference Hamiltonian D = H⊗I − I⊗H, plus a classical energy shift via a single-qubit phase rotation.
- A Laurent-QSP "soft energy comparator" of degree O((α_H/γ+1)log(1/ζ)) that flags, with error ζ, whether the candidate register's energy is lower than the anchor's by at least γ — without ever estimating either energy.
- Two algorithms, SD (fresh copies, Õ(α_H/(γη)) queries, Õ(1/η) copies) and CSD (coherent U_ψ access, Õ(α_H/(γ√η))), the latter matching Somma–de Wolf's Ω(α_H log(1/ξ)/(γ√η)) lower bound.
- Extensions to ground-state property and energy estimation with explicit complexities.

**How it works** With shift s = −γ/2 and τ = π/(4(2α_H+γ/2)), all phases θ_ab = τ(E_a−E_b−γ/2) stay in [−π/4,π/4], so y = sin(2θ) monotonically encodes the energy difference with separation Δ = sin(τγ) ≥ γ/(2(2α_H+γ/2)). Laurent QSP applied directly (not controlled) to the shifted SWAP echo realizes a polynomial approximation to a shifted error function, giving witness probability ≤ ζ when E_b ≥ E_a and ≥ 1−ζ when E_a−E_b ≥ γ. Because the ground state admits no lower-energy witness, it is absorbing; any excited anchor is flipped with probability ≥ η(1−ζ) by the candidate's ground-state component alone. SD uses M = O(1/η) trials per stage and R = O(log(1/(ηξ))) stages (per-stage contraction factor 43/64); CSD replaces the measure-and-retry loop with Yoder-type fixed-point amplitude amplification, costing O(1/√η).

**Why it matters** It cleanly settles whether controlled Hamiltonian evolution is necessary for optimal GSP, and gives a concrete recipe for analog/hybrid platforms (Rydberg arrays, trapped ions, optical lattices) where only native evolution is available. The SWAP-echo trick is likely reusable wherever controlled evolution is the bottleneck.

**Caveats** Two full system registers (2n qubits) plus ancillas, and coherent SWAPs between them, are required — nontrivial on exactly the analog hardware motivating the work. Known lower bounds on α_H, γ, η are assumed; the γ-margin comparator does not resolve excited-state spacings, and the analysis of general (non-eigenstate, mixed) anchor states rests on the monotone tracking bound rather than the idealized pairwise picture. GSEE is claimed to not need a gap promise in general, but the route here goes through GSP, which does; the truncated source leaves the GSPE/GSEE measurement assumptions unverified here. Input-state copy complexity Õ(1/η) for SD is not claimed optimal.

title: Clifford-hierarchy stabilizer formalism with applications to twisted quantum doubles
abstract: Recent work has shown that quantum double models can be used to circumvent the Bravyi-Koenig bound. In particular, this is achieved through code-switching protocols in which non-Pauli stabilizer phases appear as intermediate codes. We introduce the $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer formalism, which generalizes the Pauli stabilizer formalism by combining Pauli-$X$ operators with diagonal operators drawn from a fixed level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy on prime-dimensional qudits. This yields a natural class of beyond-Pauli stabilizer models, including many twisted quantum double phases. We classify a large class of these $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer states, showing that they are uniform superpositions over affine-linear subspaces with diagonal phases. In particular, when the stabilizers of a state require operators from level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy, we show that the diagonal gates required to produce the phases in the wavefunction sit one level higher. We further show that every 2D twisted quantum double ${\cal D}^ω(\mathbb{Z}_p^n)$ with $ω$ a product of type-III cocycles and $p$ an odd prime admits a realization using only Clifford ($k=2$) stabilizers, and we conjecture that phases where $ω$ contains a type-I or type-II cocycle require level-$p$ Clifford-hierarchy stabilizers for $p$-dimensional qudits. Finally, we demonstrate that a pair of qudit toric codes may be deterministically prepared in a logical magic state by measuring $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizers. Together, these results provide a concrete stabilizer framework for topological codes beyond Pauli stabilizer models and their logical gates.
summary:
**TL;DR** The paper defines the $X\mathcal{C}^{(k)}_d$ ("xkcd") stabilizer formalism — stabilizer groups generated by Pauli-$X$ strings times multi-qudit *diagonal* gates from level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy on prime-dimensional qudits — and proves a structure theorem: every uniquely-stabilized state is a uniform superposition over an affine-linear subspace of $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$ decorated by a diagonal phase sitting exactly one level *higher* ($k+1$) in the hierarchy. Applying this, they show all twisted quantum doubles $\mathcal{D}^\omega(\mathbb{Z}_p^n)$ with $\omega$ a product of type-III cocycles are realizable with mere Clifford ($k=2$) stabilizers, conjecture that type-I/II twists require level $p$, and give a deterministic qudit magic-state preparation protocol via code switching.

**The big picture** Recent fault-tolerance proposals evade the no-go theorem forbidding protected non-Clifford gates in two-dimensional topological codes by switching through intermediate codes whose stabilizers are not Pauli operators. Until now these constructions were ad hoc, with no general theory of what such codes can express. This work supplies that theory for a natural, group-closed family of beyond-Pauli stabilizers, and uses it to rank topological phases by how "non-Clifford" their stabilizers must be — finding, counterintuitively, that some phases hosting non-abelian anyons are cheaper to write down than purely abelian ones.

**Key contributions**
- Definition of the $X\mathcal{C}^{(k)}_d$ group $G^{(k),n}=\{X(\mathbf v)D[f]\}$, closed under multiplication even though level $k>2$ of the hierarchy is not a group; strictly generalizes XS and XP formalisms (qubits, on-site phases) to qudits and multi-site diagonal gates, and is strictly more structured than monomial stabilizer codes.
- Structure theorem (Thm. 1): $|\psi\rangle\in\Psi^{(k),n}_G$ iff $|\psi\rangle\propto\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathbb{Z}_p^\ell}e^{2\pi i\varphi(\mathbf x)}|\mathbf x, M\mathbf x+\mathbf c\rangle$ with $D[\varphi]\in\mathcal{C}^{(k+1)}_d$ — a direct generalization of the Dehaene–De Moor normal form for Pauli stabilizer states. Plus an explicit algorithm returning this canonical form from the stabilizer group.
- Constructive proof that type-III-twisted doubles $\mathcal{D}^\omega(\mathbb{Z}_p^n)$ are Clifford-stabilizer realizable ($k=2$ is tight, since non-abelian anyons exclude $k=1$), and Conjecture: $k=p$ otherwise.
- Deterministic (vs. probabilistic in the qubit case of Davydova et al.) logical magic-state preparation on two qudit toric codes via $X\mathcal{C}^{(k)}_d$ measurement.

**How it works** Diagonal hierarchy elements are parameterized as $D_m[f]$ with $f$ a polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$, level $=(m-1)(p-1)+\deg f$ (Cui–Gottesman–Krishna). The classification proceeds by showing the diagonal subgroup $D_H\trianglelefteq H$ is normal; the wavefunction support $V_\psi$ is exactly the mutual $+1$ eigenspace of $D_H$ (a "flatness" condition generalizing lattice-gauge zero-flux constraints), and the coset transversal $H/D_H$ is in bijection with $\mathbf v\in\mathbb{Z}_p^n$, forcing $V_\psi$ to be affine-linear. The level shift follows from the fact that finite differencing $\Delta_{\mathbf e_i}\phi$ lowers hierarchy level by one — conjugating $X$ by $D[\phi]$ produces a level-$k$ stabilizer from a level-$(k+1)$ phase.

**Why it matters** Gives a Haah-style classification program a concrete foothold beyond Pauli stabilizers, a practical test for whether a given wavefunction (e.g. a candidate topological ground state) is an $X\mathcal{C}^{(k)}_d$ state and at what minimal $k$, and a resource-theoretic ordering of TQD phases by stabilizer non-Cliffordness relevant to code-switching cost. Relevant to anyone designing non-Clifford logical gates or classifying commuting-projector models.

**Caveats** The $k=p$ half of the main conjecture is unproven (evidence only); the classification is for uniquely-stabilized states (higher-dimensional codespaces, i.e. codes on a torus, are handled only by adding logicals to $\mathcal{S}$); results are restricted to prime $p$ and to abelian gauge group $\mathbb{Z}_p^n$; and no error-correction properties (distance, thresholds, decoders) of $X\mathcal{C}^{(k)}_d$ codes are developed here.
